348	# Claude only: Codex maintains no equivalent usage counters, which
349	# `data/harness_capabilities.json` records as plugin_usage_counters = 0. No
350	# matcher, so it fires on every session start rather than only inside a flow
351	# project — the counters are user-level state and gating on a project manifest
352	# would record history from only the directories that happen to carry one.
353	[[claude.hooks]]
354	name = "flow-plugin-usage"
355	event = "SessionStart"
356	type = "command"
357	script = "flow-plugin-usage.sh"
358	timeout = 10
359	
360	# [[codex.hooks]] entries use the same shape (name/event/matcher/type/script,
361	# optional timeout/status_message). They deploy scripts to hook_dir and merge
362	# handler entries into hooks_file (.codex/hooks.json) under the same
363	# preserve-unmanaged contract as Claude's settings.json — config.toml is
364	# never touched. matcher is optional for Codex: omitted means match-everything.
365	
366	[[claude.hooks]]
367	name = "flow-token-verdict"
368	event = "Stop"
369	type = "command"
370	script = "flow-token-verdict.sh"
371	timeout = 15
372	status_message = "checking context carry"
373	
374	[[claude.hooks]]
375	name = "flow-context-warning"
376	event = "UserPromptSubmit"
377	type = "command"

390	name = "flow-context-warning"
391	event = "UserPromptSubmit"
392	type = "command"
393	script = "flow-context-warning.sh"
394	timeout = 10
395	
396	# The overlay-commit nudge. Registered on UserPromptSubmit rather than Stop
397	# because Stop's stdout reaches the transcript, not the model — the same
398	# constraint that makes flow-token-verdict.sh write a file instead of print.
399	# PostToolUse catches the edit while it is fresh; UserPromptSubmit catches
400	# whatever is still outstanding at the next turn boundary. Silent unless the
401	# overlay is a repo with something to commit, so this costs nothing for
402	# anyone who has not opted in.
403	
404	[[claude.hooks]]
405	name = "flow-overlay-reminder"
406	event = "PostToolUse"
407	matcher = "Write|Edit"
408	type = "command"
409	script = "flow-overlay-reminder.sh"
410	timeout = 10

412	[[claude.hooks]]
413	name = "flow-overlay-reminder"
414	event = "UserPromptSubmit"
415	type = "command"
416	script = "flow-overlay-reminder.sh"
417	timeout = 10
418	
419	# No matcher on the Codex side, deliberately. Sampling real Codex transcripts
420	# under ~/.codex/sessions shows its tool names are `exec` and friends, not
421	# `Write`/`Edit` — a Claude-shaped matcher here would never match, and the
422	# nudge would be silently dead on this runtime. Matching everything is the
423	# safe direction because `flow overlay check --hook` resolves the repo root
424	# first and exits after one cheap git call for anything irrelevant.
425	[[codex.hooks]]
426	name = "flow-overlay-reminder"
427	event = "PostToolUse"
428	type = "command"

430	timeout = 10

[framework]
name = "flow"
version = 1

[project]
flow_dir = ".flow"
source_of_truth = ".flow"

[expertise_advisory]
enabled = true

# Semantic agent capability intent is resolved once, after the framework and
# user agent inventory is merged, then translated by each runtime adapter.
[agent_capabilities.web_research]
default = true
authorization = "explicit-task-or-brief"

# Per-agent exceptions are keyed independently from [[agents]], so an overlay
# that replaces an agent body cannot erase a lower-layer denial by omission.
# Every exception, including an intentional re-enable, requires a rationale.
#
# [[agent_capability_overrides]]
# agent = "example-local-only-role"
# capability = "web_research"
# enabled = false
# rationale = "This role must remain local-only."

# Declared dependencies on upstream standards. Each block names the upstream
# source, the version flow is pinned to, and where the verbatim vendor mirror
# lives. Run `scripts/refresh-conventional-commits.py` to roll a vendor forward.
[standards.git-commits]
spec = "Conventional Commits"
upstream = "https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/"
upstream_repo = "https://github.com/conventional-commits/conventionalcommits.org"
upstream_version = "v1.0.0"
upstream_license = "MIT"
vendored_path = "standards/vendor/conventional-commits-1.0.0.md"
vendored_sha = "7d293dc59e88abc8ce6c6698344d4da518ff3f27"
vendored_at = "2026-05-15"
flow_standard = "standards/git-commits.md"

[claude]
skill_dir = ".claude/skills"
agent_dir = ".claude/agents"
hook_dir = ".claude/hooks"
settings_file = ".claude/settings.json"
managed_manifest = ".claude/flow.managed.toml"

[claude.skill_defaults]
disable_model_invocation = true
argument_hint = "[focus]"

[claude.agent_defaults]
generation_mode = "verbatim"

[claude.settings]
preserve_unmanaged = true
manage_hooks = true
manage_settings_file = true

[codex]
skill_dir = ".agents/skills"
agent_dir = ".codex/agents"

[codex.skill_defaults]
argument_hint = "[focus]"

[model_tiers.judgment.claude]

[model_tiers.working.claude]

[model_tiers.mechanical.claude]

[session_model_profiles.mechanical]
description = "Mechanical transformations and routine administrative work with clear outcomes."

event = "SessionStart"

1	# flow-help
2	
3	Show the flow framework overview: phase machine, command catalog, agent roster, and architecture summary.
4	
5	## Overview
6	
7	This command is the framework's discoverable entry point. Use it to answer "what does flow do?" and "which command or agent fits this task?" without re-reading every command contract.
8	
9	## When to Use
10	
11	Use this command when:
12	
13	- you want to remember which command does what
14	- you're new to flow and want orientation
15	- you want to look up an agent role without re-reading the framework docs
16	- you want to show a collaborator how the framework is shaped
17	
18	**When NOT to use:** to learn the full workflow inside a specific command. Those phases live in each command's own contract. `flow-help` is the orientation surface.
19	
20	## Primary inputs
21	
22	- the framework's own identity (this file + FRAMEWORK.md)
23	- no project state required; `flow-help` is intentionally project-agnostic
24	
25	## Primary outputs
26	
27	- a one-screen orientation including phase machine, command catalog, agent roster, architecture summary, and pointers to deeper docs
28	
29	## Help Workflow
30	
31	1. State the framework's one-line identity.
32	2. Render the phase machine diagram.
33	3. List the available commands with one-line "use when" guidance.
34	4. List the available agents with one-line role descriptions and the core+conditional invocation pattern.
35	5. Summarize architecture (user-level vs project-level; runtime memory provider vs STATE.md vs runs).
36	6. List common entry points by intent ("Start a fresh session" → /flow-boot, etc.).
37	7. Point at deeper docs (`FRAMEWORK.md`, the maintainer docs at `~/.flow/source/docs/`).
38

# flow-help

Show the flow framework overview: phase machine, command catalog, agent roster, and architecture summary.

## Overview

This command is the framework's discoverable entry point. Use it to answer "what does flow do?" and "which command or agent fits this task?" without re-reading every command contract.

## When to Use

Use this command when:

- you want to remember which command does what
- you're new to flow and want orientation
- you want to look up an agent role without re-reading the framework docs
- you want to show a collaborator how the framework is shaped

**When NOT to use:** to learn the full workflow inside a specific command. Those phases live in each command's own contract. `flow-help` is the orientation surface.

## Primary inputs

- the framework's own identity (this file + FRAMEWORK.md)
- no project state required; `flow-help` is intentionally project-agnostic

## Primary outputs

- a one-screen orientation including phase machine, command catalog, agent roster, architecture summary, and pointers to deeper docs

## Help Workflow

1. State the framework's one-line identity.
2. Render the phase machine diagram.
3. List the available commands with one-line "use when" guidance.
4. List the available agents with one-line role descriptions and the core+conditional invocation pattern.
5. Summarize architecture (user-level vs project-level; runtime memory provider vs STATE.md vs runs).
6. List common entry points by intent ("Start a fresh session" → /flow-boot, etc.).
7. Point at deeper docs (`FRAMEWORK.md`, the maintainer docs at `~/.flow/source/docs/`).

## Output Format

**Always emit your result in the following format before ending the command.** Do not stop after gathering inputs — produce the output.

```md
## flow Framework

Personal AI workflow framework. It defines HOW Claude and Codex operate with you, not WHAT you work on. Active in every supported runtime session through the user-level install.

## Phase machine

boot ──┬─→ scout (XS/S, narrow) ────────────────────────────→ archive
       │                                                      ↑
       └─→ define ──→ [solution] ──→ plan ──→ implement (gated) ──→ review ┘
                                                     ↑
                                                     └── resume (recover from interruption)

`define` turns early feature or architectural-capability ideas into approved requirements. `[solution]` is an optional pre-plan step after definition; use it when multiple approaches exist, architectural decisions are needed, or the work needs chunking before `plan` can shape it. Bug-shaped work can go directly to `/flow-plan`.

## Command surfaces

Flow has **two distinct command surfaces** — invoke each differently:

### Workflow commands

These are the commands you use during work. Claude exposes them as slash commands (`/flow-XXX`). Codex receives the same command bodies as skills.

<!-- generated:slash-commands-table:begin (regenerate with `scripts/regenerate-flow-help.py`) -->

<!-- generated:slash-commands-table:end -->

<!-- generated:cli-commands-table:begin (regenerate with `scripts/regenerate-flow-help.py`) -->

<!-- generated:cli-commands-table:end -->

The table above is derived from `[[help.cli_commands]]` in `flow.toml`.

## Agents

13 working agents. Light commands (boot, scout, resume, status, help) skip them. Heavier commands (define, solution, plan, implement, review, archive) use a **core trio + conditional specialists** pattern: core agents always engage, and conditional agents join when their concern applies.

<!-- generated:agents-table:begin (regenerate with `scripts/regenerate-flow-help.py`) -->
| Agent | Role |
|---|---|
| architect | Boundaries, integrations, ADR decisions |
| business-analyst | Problem framing, acceptance criteria |
| data-engineer | Persistent state changes, schema, migration |
| lead-developer | Execution planning, slice sequencing |
| product-manager | Scope, prioritization, tradeoff framing |
| quality-reviewer | Pre-acceptance review of any deliverable (code, docs, analyses, runbooks) |
| security-reviewer | Sensitive surfaces, secrets, auth |
| solution-architect | Consulting design partner — walks options, tradeoffs, principles, and recommended design artifacts before plan |
| sre | Rollout, runtime, observability |
| support-lead | Operator-facing notes, troubleshooting |
| tech-writer | Durable summary, memory wording, handback |
| test-engineer | Coverage strategy, validation depth |
| ux-specialist | Interaction states, accessibility |
<!-- generated:agents-table:end -->

The table above is derived from shared `[[agents]]` `summary` fields in `flow.toml` (agents are sorted by `name`).

### How agents get invoked

- **By commands**: `flow-define`, `flow-solution`, `flow-plan`, `flow-implement`, `flow-review`, and `flow-archive` invoke agents from their composition. See each command's "Composition" section for which agents are core vs conditional.
- **Directly**: ask the runtime to engage a specific role for a focused task, for example "have the architect look at this boundary decision" or "use the quality-reviewer to check this PR".

### Agent vs distribution-tool distinction

These agents are **personal working agents**. They define how Claude or Codex works with you when it plays a specific role. They are NOT distribution outputs designed for others to install. Project-specific review tools, such as path-nexus's review agents in `tools/agents/`, live in their project's own distribution surface.

## Architecture

- "Where do we stand?" → `/flow-status`
```

1	#!/usr/bin/env python3
2	"""Regenerate Flow help tables from flow.toml.
3	
4	Tables are generated between `<!-- generated:<name>:begin -->` /
5	`<!-- generated:<name>:end -->` markers. The command and agent tables live in
6	flow-help.md; README.md receives the same CLI command table:
7	
8	  - slash-commands-table — from `[[claude.commands]]` `summary` fields,
9	    in the order they appear in flow.toml
10	  - cli-commands-table — from `[[help.cli_commands]]` entries
11	  - agents-table — from shared `[[agents]]` `summary` fields, sorted by name
12	
13	Why: the hand-maintained tables drifted twice in successive feature commits
14	during the v0.4.0 → v0.4.1 cycle. Generating from `flow.toml` makes the
15	manifest the single source of truth and eliminates the drift class.
16	
17	Usage:
18	  python3 scripts/regenerate-flow-help.py            # write changes
19	  python3 scripts/regenerate-flow-help.py --check    # exit 1 if regeneration would change anything
20	"""
21	from __future__ import annotations
22	
23	import argparse
24	import difflib
25	import re
26	import sys
27	from pathlib import Path
28	
29	import tomllib
30	
31	REPO_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
32	FLOW_TOML = REPO_ROOT / "scaffolds" / "default" / "flow.toml"
33	FLOW_HELP = REPO_ROOT / "scaffolds" / "default" / "commands" / "flow-help.md"
34	README = REPO_ROOT / "README.md"
35	
36	
37	def read_toml(path: Path) -> dict:
38	    """Read a manifest using stdlib tomllib.
39	
40	    Requires Python 3.11+, unlike the CLI, which supports 3.10 and carries a
41	    fallback parser in `cli/flowtoml.py` for it. This is a dev-only tool that
42	    rewrites files in `scaffolds/`; it never runs on an end user's machine, so
43	    it does not have to honour the CLI's supported-interpreter floor. The copy
44	    of that fallback parser that used to live here was dead code on every
45	    interpreter that actually ran it.
46	    """
47	    return tomllib.loads(path.read_text())
48	
49	
50	def escape_cell(text: str) -> str:
51	    """Escape `|` so it stays inside its cell.
52	
53	    A raw pipe ends a GitHub table cell even inside backticks, so an
54	    invocation such as `all|claude|codex` would otherwise split its row.
55	    GitHub renders `\\|` as a literal pipe in both places.
56	    """
57	    return text.replace("|", "\\|")
58	
59	
60	def render_table(rows: list[tuple[str, str]], headers: tuple[str, str]) -> str:
61	    h1, h2 = headers
62	    lines = [f"| {h1} | {h2} |", "|---|---|"]
63	    for col1, col2 in rows:
64	        lines.append(f"| {escape_cell(col1)} | {escape_cell(col2)} |")
65	    return "\n".join(lines)
66	
67	
68	def build_slash_commands_table(data: dict) -> str:
69	    commands = data.get("claude", {}).get("commands", [])
70	    rows: list[tuple[str, str]] = []
71	    for cmd in commands:
72	        name = cmd.get("name", "")
73	        summary = cmd.get("summary")
74	        if not summary:
75	            raise SystemExit(
76	                f"flow.toml [[claude.commands]] entry missing `summary`: name={name!r}\n"
77	                "add a one-line summary suitable for the flow-help command table."
78	            )
79	        rows.append((f"/{name}", summary))
80	    return render_table(rows, ("Command", "Use when"))
81	
82	
83	def build_cli_commands_table(data: dict) -> str:
84	    entries = data.get("help", {}).get("cli_commands", [])
85	    rows: list[tuple[str, str]] = []
86	    for entry in entries:
87	        invocation = entry.get("invocation", "")
88	        summary = entry.get("summary")
89	        if not invocation:
90	            raise SystemExit("flow.toml [[help.cli_commands]] entry missing `invocation`")
91	        if not summary:
92	            raise SystemExit(
93	                f"flow.toml [[help.cli_commands]] entry missing `summary`: invocation={invocation!r}"
94	            )
95	        rows.append((f"`{invocation}`", summary))
96	    return render_table(rows, ("Command", "Use when"))
97	
98	
99	def build_agents_table(data: dict) -> str:
100	    agents = data.get("agents", [])
101	    rows: list[tuple[str, str]] = []
102	    for agent in sorted(agents, key=lambda a: a.get("name", "")):
103	        name = agent.get("name", "")
104	        summary = agent.get("summary")
105	        if not summary:
106	            raise SystemExit(
107	                f"flow.toml [[agents]] entry missing `summary`: name={name!r}\n"
108	                "add a one-line summary suitable for the flow-help agents table."
109	            )
110	        rows.append((name, summary))
111	    return render_table(rows, ("Agent", "Role"))
112	
113	
114	BUILDERS = {
115	    "slash-commands-table": build_slash_commands_table,
116	    "cli-commands-table": build_cli_commands_table,
117	    "agents-table": build_agents_table,
118	}
119	
120	
121	def replace_section(text: str, marker: str, content: str, *, target: Path = FLOW_HELP) -> str:
122	    """Replace the body between `<!-- generated:<marker>:begin ... -->` and `<!-- generated:<marker>:end -->`."""
123	    begin_re = re.compile(rf"(<!-- generated:{re.escape(marker)}:begin[^>]*-->)")
124	    end_re = re.compile(rf"(<!-- generated:{re.escape(marker)}:end -->)")
125	
126	    begin_match = begin_re.search(text)
127	    if not begin_match:
128	        raise SystemExit(f"could not find begin marker for {marker} in {target.name}")
129	    end_match = end_re.search(text, begin_match.end())
130	    if not end_match:
131	        raise SystemExit(
132	            f"could not find end marker for {marker} in {target.name} "
133	            f"(after begin at {begin_match.start()})"
134	        )
135	
136	    return (
137	        text[: begin_match.end()]
138	        + "\n"
139	        + content
140	        + "\n"
141	        + text[end_match.start():]
142	    )
143	
144	
145	def main() -> int:
146	    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
147	        description=__doc__,
148	        formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter,
149	    )
150	    parser.add_argument(
151	        "--check",
152	        action="store_true",
153	        help="exit 1 with a diff if regeneration would change generated help targets; do not write",
154	    )
155	    args = parser.parse_args()
156	
157	    if not FLOW_TOML.exists():
158	        sys.stderr.write(f"flow.toml not found at {FLOW_TOML}\n")
159	        return 1
160	    data = read_toml(FLOW_TOML)
161	    targets = {
162	        FLOW_HELP: tuple(BUILDERS),
163	        README: ("cli-commands-table",),
164	    }
165	    stale: list[tuple[Path, str, str]] = []
166	    for target, markers in targets.items():
167	        if not target.exists():
168	            sys.stderr.write(f"generated help target not found at {target}\n")
169	            return 1
170	        original = target.read_text()
171	        rewritten = original
172	        for marker in markers:
173	            rewritten = replace_section(
174	                rewritten, marker, BUILDERS[marker](data), target=target
175	            )
176	        if rewritten != original:
177	            stale.append((target, original, rewritten))
178	
179	    if not stale:
180	        for target in targets:
181	            print(f"{target.relative_to(REPO_ROOT)} is up to date.")
182	        return 0
183	
184	    if args.check:
185	        for target, original, rewritten in stale:
186	            sys.stderr.write(
187	                "".join(
188	                    difflib.unified_diff(
189	                        original.splitlines(keepends=True),
190	                        rewritten.splitlines(keepends=True),
191	                        fromfile=str(target.relative_to(REPO_ROOT)) + " (on disk)",
192	                        tofile=str(target.relative_to(REPO_ROOT)) + " (regenerated)",
193	                    )
194	                )
195	            )
196	        sys.stderr.write("\ngenerated Flow help is out of date.\n")
197	        sys.stderr.write("run `python3 scripts/regenerate-flow-help.py` to apply.\n")
198	        return 1
199	
200	    for target, _original, rewritten in stale:
201	        target.write_text(rewritten)
202	        print(f"updated {target.relative_to(REPO_ROOT)}")
203	    return 0
204	
205	
206	if __name__ == "__main__":
207	    raise SystemExit(main())

README.md

1	# flow CLI Reference
2	
3	## Overview
4	
5	`flow` manages six things:
6	
7	- machine-local install support
8	- project-local `.flow` scaffolding
9	- runtime adapter generation and drift detection
10	- token usage: reading both harnesses' local transcripts into a store, and reading it back
11	- version control for the user overlay at `~/.flow/user/`
12	- local agent-expertise retrieval, admission, evaluation evidence, and runtime diagnostics
13	
14	Three **hook entry points** exist only to be called by generated hooks — `flow cost verdict --hook`, `flow cost warn --hook`, and `flow overlay check --hook`. They read hook JSON on stdin and are documented here for anyone reading a `settings.json` entry and wondering what it invokes, not because there is a reason to type them. (`flow cost verdict` also has an interactive `--transcript` mode, which is worth typing.)
15	
16	The usage-tracking commands form a pipeline, and the order matters: **`harvest` writes raw records → `normalize` projects them into one token convention → `cost` reads the normalized layer.** `flow cost active` and `flow cost verdict` run the needed harvest/normalize work for the current surface; `flow cost summary`, `flow cost sessions`, `flow cost trend`, and `flow cost baseline` stay read-only and label freshness so stale data does not look current.
17	
18	## Command Reference
19	
20	### `flow setup machine`
21	
22	Prepare machine-local support under `~/.flow`.
23	
24	Creates:
25	
26	- `~/.flow/config.toml`
27	- `~/.flow/hooks/`
28	- `~/.flow/user/`
29	- `~/.flow/logs/`
30	
31	Use this when setting up a new machine or repairing a missing local install surface.
32	
33	### `flow setup project`
34	
35	Scaffold `repo/.flow` into the current repository.
36	
37	Behavior:
38	
39	- creates exactly four paths: `flow.toml`, `PROJECT.md`, `memory/STATE.md`, and `runs/.gitkeep`
40	- does not overwrite files that already exist
41	- copies no commands, agents, standards, templates, or `FRAMEWORK.md`. Those are framework capability, served by the user-level install; copying them into a repo produced a fork that never updated. A project set up before this change can be reconciled with `flow project migrate`.
42	
43	Use this when bootstrapping a repo for the first time.
44	
45	### `flow setup user`
46	
47	Install flow at the **user level** so it is active in every supported runtime session regardless of cwd.
48	
49	Behavior:
50	
51	- runs `flow sync claude --user` and `flow sync codex --user` in sequence
52	- generates `~/.claude/skills/flow-*/`, `~/.claude/agents/*.md`, `~/.claude/hooks/flow-*.sh`
53	- generates `~/.agents/skills/flow-*/`, `~/.codex/agents/*.toml`, `~/.codex/hooks/flow-*.sh`
54	- merges flow hook entries into `~/.claude/settings.json` (preserves unmanaged settings)
55	- writes `~/.claude/flow.managed.toml`, `~/.codex/hooks.json`, and `~/.codex/flow.managed.toml` for hook registration and drift tracking
56	
57	Use this once per machine, then again whenever the framework scaffold changes and you want the user-level surface to follow.
58	
59	### `flow refresh project`
60	
61	**Retired.** Exits 1 and points at the commands that took over.
62	
63	It repaired a missing manifest and missing core files, and restored manifest-declared sources from the scaffold. The first two are things `flow setup project` already does idempotently; the third is fork restoration in miniature, and is what `flow project migrate` exists to undo. A project overlay no longer holds framework files, so there is nothing left for it to refresh.
64	
65	| what it used to do | what to run |
66	|---|---|
67	| missing `flow.toml` or core files | `flow setup project` |
68	| framework copies still present | `flow project audit`, then `flow project migrate` |
69	
70	**One capability has no successor.** Updating an *existing* `PROJECT.md` or `memory/STATE.md` from the framework template is gone — `copy_if_missing` never touches a file that is there, and nothing else offers the update. Those files are the project's own content from the moment it is initialized, so edit them directly. The retirement message says this rather than leaving it to be discovered.
71	
72	The refusal fires before any filesystem check, including whether `.flow` exists. Someone typing a retired command needs to hear that it is retired, not a setup error about a directory the command would no longer have touched.
73	
74	### `flow bootstrap`
75	
76	Validate that the minimum `repo/.flow` structure exists.
77	
78	Checks for:
79	
80	- `flow.toml`
81	- `PROJECT.md`
82	- `memory/`
83	
84	It reports absent `commands/`, `agents/`, `standards/`, `project/`, and `templates/` directories as optional. The user-level install provides framework commands and agents unless the project overlay registers local replacements.
85	
86	Use this after scaffold or when diagnosing a broken repo state.
87	
88	### `flow help`
89	
90	Print the framework orientation: workflow phases, slash commands, CLI commands, agents, and architecture.
91	
92	Same content as the `/flow-help` slash command. Use this at a shell when you are not inside a Claude session.
93	
94	### `flow run list`
95	
96	List workflow runs under the current repo's `.flow/runs/` directory.
97	
98	Flags:
99	
100	- `--all` — include archived runs
101	- `--json` — emit JSON
102	
103	Runs with `run.json` are C-lite runs. Existing artifact folders without `run.json` are reported as `legacy/inferred`; reading them does not create state.
104	
105	### `flow run status <work-id>`
106	
107	Show one run's current state.
108	
109	Flags:
110	
111	- `--json` — emit JSON
112	
113	For C-lite runs, this reads `.flow/runs/<work-id>/run.json`. For legacy run folders, it reports `legacy/inferred` and lists discovered artifacts.
114	
115	### `flow run history <work-id>`
116	
117	Show one run's append-only transition history from `.flow/runs/<work-id>/events.jsonl`.
118	
119	Flags:
120	
121	- `--json` — emit JSON
122	
123	Legacy/inferred runs may have no history; that is reported as an empty event list rather than creating one.
124	
125	### `flow run verify <work-id>`
126	
127	Check a run's state/history consistency.
128	
129	Flags:
130	
131	- `--json` — emit JSON
132	
133	For C-lite runs, verification checks schema version, presence of transition history, latest event state, and `last_event`. For legacy/inferred runs, verification succeeds with the explicit message `legacy/inferred: no canonical run.json`.
134	
135	### `flow run validate-orchestration <work-id> --stage <stage>`
136	
137	Read-only validation of `.flow/runs/<work-id>/orchestration.json`.
138	
139	Flags:
140	
141	- `--stage dispatch|handback|acceptance` — required cumulative validation stage
142	- `--json` — emit stable `ok`, `stage`, `manifest`, and `findings` fields
143	
144	Dispatch checks briefs, evidence inventories, declared capabilities, output ownership, risk, and concurrency. Handback adds outputs, reconciliation, baseline, recovery, readback, comparison, and unexpected-delta checks. Acceptance adds identity provenance and high-risk verifier independence. Diagnostics identify the field, subject, rule, and corrective action without printing referenced artifact contents.
145	
146	The command validates declarations. It cannot query hidden runtime grants, prove semantic truth, or establish transactional behavior for arbitrary external systems.
147	
148	### `flow run execute-local <work-id>`
149	
150	Start one local `test-engineer` execution attempt through an optional supervised Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) process. Flow owns the policy gate, physical Ollama call, execution ledger, and sealed receipt; MAF proposes the specialist action and coordinates the result. This command does not advance the C-lite lifecycle.
151	
152	```sh
153	flow run execute-local WORK_ID --assignment ASSIGNMENT_ID \
154	  --task-file .flow/runs/WORK_ID/local-task.txt --json
155	```
156	
157	The run must be revision 2 and `implementing`, with a valid `orchestration.json`. The selected `test-engineer` assignment must declare `execution.provider = "ollama"` and a local `execution.model`. The task file must live inside that run and is limited to 4096 bytes. The command returns an attempt ID, status, receipt path, and reason. An interrupted physical call is `unknown` and is never retried automatically. A failed start or denial receives a no-dispatch receipt. Paid providers are disabled.
158	
159	MAF is optional: ordinary Flow commands do not import it. For this first slice, install the pinned runner requirements in a separate Python environment and set `FLOW_MAF_PYTHON` to that environment's Python executable before calling `execute-local`. See `runtime/maf_runner/requirements.txt`. A configured local Ollama server and model are required for a physical worker call. The receipt and ledger live under `.flow/runs/WORK_ID/execution/`; a receipt reports observed facts and does not itself approve lifecycle handback.
160	
161	For the bounded multi-turn exercise, add `--multi-turn`. Flow then records three ordered action positions and three separate replan decisions. The first two replans may be allowed; the third is denied by the two-replan cap and ends that MAF phase. Flow checks the denial state before starting an independent action-3 phase in the same attempt. `--interrupt-after-third-send` is an exercise-only fault point: it marks the third action `unknown` immediately after Flow records `adapter_send_started`, before calling Ollama. The first two actions still make physical Ollama calls. This flag does not prove that Ollama received the third request. Inspect the v2 receipt and checkpoint positions for the evidence actually recorded. For a disposable loopback arrival observer, set `FLOW_OLLAMA_OBSERVER=1`, `FLOW_OLLAMA_URL=http://127.0.0.1:PORT/api/chat`, and `FLOW_OLLAMA_OBSERVER_LOG` to its owner-only JSONL file inside the run. The receipt seals a per-action arrival table; without an observer it labels endpoint arrival evidence unavailable.
162	
163	### `flow run execute-chartered-job <work-id> --worktree PATH --source-commit COMMIT`
164	
165	Run an approved charter-selected specialist roster through Flow-gated Magentic, for the revision-2 implementing run.
166	
167	```sh
168	flow run execute-chartered-job WORK_ID --worktree PATH --source-commit COMMIT [--project-root PATH] [--json]
169	```
170	
171	The run must be revision 2 and `implementing`, with a valid dispatch-stage `orchestration.json`. The approved `job-charter.json` must be linked through that orchestration manifest — the `magentic-manager` assignment's `input_evidence` must name the charter, or the run's declared `job_charter` artifact must match it. The charter pins the task, read/write paths, test, baseline, and the producer and verifier instance IDs drawn from the manifest's roster.
172	
173	Direct Claude and Codex edits are Flow-gated: only specialists the charter names as producers may hold edit capability, and their write scope must equal the charter's declared `write_paths`. Ollama performs read-only verification only — an Ollama-backed specialist must be read-only, and every declared verifier must be an independent read-only specialist disjoint from the producers. Native subagents are disabled; the roster runs only the Flow-approved specialists bound in the orchestration manifest.
174	
175	### `flow run inspect-execution <work-id> <attempt-id>`
176	
177	Read the original envelope, action, ordered ledger events, source snapshot checks, checkpoint link, receipt, and missing evidence without creating a new attempt or calling a provider. Use `--json` for structured output. Recovery decisions use the Flow ledger; a missing local response is an unknown outcome, not proof that Ollama did not receive the request.
178	
179	### `flow run inspect-delivery <work-id> [--attempt-id <id>]`
180	
181	Read the current Flow-owned Shaper-to-Delivery authority and, when present, one execution attempt. With no attempt ID, Flow selects the newest attempt directory that contains an envelope. The command does not grant, resume, or dispatch work.
182	
183	The JSON view reports lifecycle state, the sealed charter and owner generation, protocol compatibility diagnostics, and the v7 attempt's current execution and resume eligibility. Historical v6 envelopes remain readable evidence but always report `executable: false` and `resumable: false`; create a new sealed Delivery Charter for new work.
184	
185	### `flow run resume-execution <work-id> <attempt-id>`
186	
187	Fence the previous parent and reopen the same attempt. An uncertain dispatch returns `reconciliation_required` without a provider send. The v1 path can replay one committed result through a bound MAF checkpoint. For v2, a completed first or second action can be replayed through its verified pending checkpoint in a fresh MAF process; Flow reuses committed results and decisions and authorizes only the next logical action. A missing, changed, or incompatible checkpoint halts as a runtime protocol gap. A matching receipt written before the ledger's terminal update is repaired without dispatch. An unresolved third action always halts pending reconciliation. This command never allocates a replacement attempt.
188	
189	### `flow run resolve-execution <work-id> <attempt-id> <action-id>`
190	
191	Append an operator resolution using `--actor`, `--disposition`, `--explanation`, and `--evidence-file`. The evidence file contains a JSON list of `{ "kind": "...", "path": ".flow/runs/.../execution/.../file", "sha256": "..." }` records; each referenced file must exist inside the original attempt directory and match its digest. Flow copies bounded proof bytes into an owner-only, read-only attempt directory and checks their hashes on inspection. Completion requires a durable validated response observation. No-dispatch is permitted only before Flow's dispatch boundary. `still_unknown` records the investigation and leaves dispatch blocked.
192	
193	### `flow run continue-resolved-execution <work-id> <attempt-id> <action-id>`
194	
195	Continue an evidence-resolved third action with `--actor` for local operator attribution. The command requires the original terminal receipt, exact resolution, and a verified `pending_delegate:3` checkpoint. Pinned MAF must restore that checkpoint and report the same pending action before Flow considers a new send. `resolved_completed` replays the durable result without a provider call; `resolved_not_dispatched` requires a fresh policy grant and makes at most one send. Flow writes a separate linked continuation receipt; the original receipt remains unchanged. A failed readiness check halts without a send, and an uncertain post-send response remains `unknown`. The local OS file permission boundary controls access; actor text is attribution, not authentication.
196	
197	### `flow run transition <work-id> <event>`
198	
199	Apply a hard-gated lifecycle transition. Invalid transitions and orchestration refusals leave `run.json` and `events.jsonl` unchanged.
200	
201	Flags:
202	
203	- `--artifact NAME=PATH` — record gate evidence or an artifact pointer; may be repeated
204	- `--disposition NAME=VALUE` — record a closure disposition; may be repeated
205	- `--note TEXT` — record a next action or transition note
206	- `--json` — emit JSON
207	
208	Core path events:
209	
210	- `start-definition`
211	- `approve-definition` — requires `--artifact requirements=...` and `--artifact acceptance_criteria=...`
212	- `start-solution`
213	- `approve-solution` — requires `--artifact solution=...` and `--disposition risk=...`
214	- `start-plan`
215	
216	For revision-2 runs, `approve-definition` must record `requirements`, `acceptance_criteria`, and a reviewed `shaper_intent` JSON artifact. The intent file carries the per-run problem, users, outcomes, boundaries, approvals, and exact effective specialist-definition digests. `start-plan` fails closed if any source is missing or outside the current run; it never infers those semantics from Markdown or substitutes framework defaults.
217	- `approve-plan` — requires `--artifact plan=...`, `--artifact handoff=...`, and `--artifact validation_plan=...`
218	- `start-implementation`
219	- `mark-handback-ready` — requires `--artifact implementation_evidence=...` and `--artifact handback=...`
220	- `start-review`
221	- `accept-review` — requires `--artifact review=...`
222	- `archive` — requires `--disposition capability_gaps=...` and `--disposition memory=...`
223	
224	Support events:
225	
226	- `pause`
227	- `block`
228	- `resume`
229	- `archive-scout` — creates the minimal scout closure envelope and requires `--artifact scout_summary=...`, `--disposition capability_gaps=...`, and `--disposition memory=...`
230	
231	`flow run transition` is the only command that writes lifecycle state. `/flow-*` commands call it when they cross gates; they do not hand-edit `run.json`.
232	
233	New runs are protocol revision 2 while `run.json` remains schema 1. Their definition, solution, and plan approvals require `--artifact orchestration_manifest=.flow/runs/<work-id>/orchestration.json` and dispatch validation. Handback and review acceptance re-run the later stages. Runs without `protocol_revision` are revision 1 and retain the previous behavior. A scout remains lightweight unless it supplies an orchestration manifest, in which case `archive-scout` validates acceptance.
234	
235	### `flow model context`
236	
237	Collect the read-only facts used by the shared parent-session model rubric.
238	
239	```bash
240	flow model context --runtime codex --lane plan --json
241	flow model context --runtime claude --lane boot --parent-model claude-opus-5
242	```
243	
244	Required flags:
245	
246	- `--runtime claude|codex`
247	- `--lane boot|define|solution|plan|resume`
248	
249	Optional parent model and effort flags record a user declaration. CLI input
250	cannot prove same-session observation, so it remains `declared`. The JSON
251	envelope keeps profile resolution, mapping provenance, availability, active
252	parent identity, project-attributed seven-day history, global capacity, and
253	limitations separate.
254	
255	The command opens only an existing compatible usage store with SQLite
256	`mode=ro` and `query_only`. It never creates, migrates, harvests, normalizes,
257	or writes the store. Absent, partial, unreadable, incompatible, and stale
258	evidence remain explicit and never become zero consumption or a performance
259	claim.
260	
261	### `flow model resolve`
262	
263	Resolve a semantic profile after an agent assesses the work under
264	`standards/session-model-advice.md`.
265	
266	```bash
267	flow model resolve --runtime codex --profile judgment --json
268	```
269	
270	Profiles are `mechanical`, `working`, `judgment`, and `demanding`.
271	Results are `resolved`, `unresolved`, `disabled`, or `invalid`. A resolved
272	mapping reports the runtime-native model, effort, source, verification date,
273	and configuration provenance; availability remains separately qualified. The
274	command does not select a profile, call a model, switch the parent session, or
275	configure delegated agents.
276	
277	### `flow runtime smoke`
278	
279	Check generated Claude and Codex runtime adapter surfaces and list the manual
280	runtime smoke evidence still required.
281	
282	Flags:
283	
284	- `--target all|claude|codex` — runtime target to check (default: all)
285	- `--json` — emit JSON
286	
287	Static checks prove local generated files only:
288	
289	- managed manifests exist and cover desired outputs
290	- generated surfaces are fresh against the current scaffold/user-overlay manifest
291	- generated command skills exist
292	- command skills include Flow Agent Routing
293	- every routing-table row equals the effective generated-agent policy after
294	  tier, runtime-specific, and generic overrides
295	- lifecycle command skills include the C-lite run protocol text
296	- generated agents exist
297	- generated agents contain the model and effort fields resolved from `flow.toml`
298	- generated hooks exist
299	
300	Manual-required checks are intentionally not treated as failures:
301	
302	- invoke a representative command in Claude and Codex and confirm it loads
303	- invoke a low-risk role agent such as `support-lead`
304	- inspect transcript or runtime log evidence for configured model and effort
305	  where the runtime exposes it
306	
307	This command is read-only. It exits 1 only when a static check fails. It does
308	not claim that local files prove the client honored model routing at runtime.
309	
310	### `flow doctor`
311	
312	Report machine, install, user-level, and project-level state in one output.
313	
314	Flags:
315	
316	- `--json` — emit the same support facts as a structured diagnostic payload.
317	- `--check` — exit nonzero when any error- or warning-severity diagnostic is present.
318	
319	Current sections:
320	
321	- **machine** — Python, flow home, source path, scaffold availability, config, launcher
322	- **install** — install mode (develop or release), version (release only), source target (develop only), installed_at timestamp
323	- **user-level** — Claude/Codex sync state and drift for `~/.claude/`, `~/.agents/skills/`, and `~/.codex/`
324	- **project** — repo `.flow/` presence, manifest, whether the overlay still carries framework copies, how many of its files have drifted from the framework, project-local runtime adoption surfaces, each `[[replaces]]` wiring's status, and whether `PROJECT.md` still lists the retired project-standards section
325	
326	The overlay count and the drift count are reported **separately and never summed**. `overlay:` counts what `flow project migrate` removes by default and can therefore drive to zero, which is what lets that line name that command. `drifted:` counts files that differ from the framework, which is not clearable the same way — removing one is opt-in and may destroy a customization. Summed, the number would name a remedy that cannot reach it, and doctor would report a permanent fault where there is none. A drifted overlay with nothing removable reads `overlay: clean` alongside a `drifted:` line, and both are true.
327	
328	The `replaces:` block appears only when the project declares wirings. Each is reported as `ok` (the replacement resolves in your user overlay), `absent` (it does not resolve *on this machine* — a wiring names a path under `~/.flow/user/` that a teammate may not have, so this is a gap in your overlay rather than a fault in the project), `unknown` (the `default` names no framework file, so the wiring can never match), or `invalid` (the entry did not validate). In `--check` mode, any warning or error diagnostic makes the command exit nonzero.
329	
330	The `adoption:` line reports project-local runtime directories that Flow does
331	not own through user-level sync. Directories such as `.claude/`, `.codex/`, and
332	`.agents/` are `unmanaged` until you remove stale generated content or declare
333	intentional project ownership in `.flow/flow.toml` with
334	`[[adoption.exclusions]]`. Invalid exclusions appear as `adoption config:` so a
335	typo does not hide a real adoption gap.

337	The JSON payload uses stable diagnostic items with `id`, `status`, `severity`, `category`, `summary`, and optional `target`, `path`, `detail`, and `next_action`. Categories include `missing`, `parse_error`, `permission_denied`, `git_unavailable`, `remote_unreachable`, `manifest_invalid`, `managed_conflict`, `runtime_not_found`, `drift`, `stale`, `manual_required`, `warning`, and `ok`.

341	### `flow install --release`
342	
343	Convert an existing develop install from symlink mode to release mode. This is mode conversion, not the normal first-install path. The clone is **not** deleted — the user controls its lifecycle.
344	
345	Behavior:
346	
347	- Resolves the symlink target as the source clone
348	- Determines version via `git describe` in the clone (exact tag → base tag + dev sha → `main@<sha>`)
349	- Copies the release roster (`cli/`, `scaffolds/`, `hooks/`, `scripts/`, `docs/`, `README.md`) into a staging directory under `~/.flow/`
350	- Validates staging. It must contain `cli/flow.py` (which has to parse), `scaffolds/default/flow.toml`, and `data/harness_capabilities.json`. Every module-scope import reachable from the staged `flow.py`, followed transitively, must also resolve — either as a file under the staged `cli/`, or as something importable from the current environment. The set is read out of the staged entrypoint rather than kept as a list in the validator, because this check runs from the *installed* version against a *newer* tree, so any hand-maintained roster would be behind by construction. Resolution rather than classification, for the same reason: an older install cannot know whether a new name is a flow module or a package flow started depending on, and guessing would let it reject a valid future release with no way to ship the correction.
351	- Atomically swaps the staging directory into `~/.flow/source/`
352	- Updates `~/.flow/config.toml` with `mode = "release"`, version, remote, and installed_at
353	
354	Use this when a contributor's machine is ready to switch off development mode and pin to copied release content.

361

363	- Removes the copied directory at `~/.flow/source/`
364	- Creates a symlink from `~/.flow/source` to the given clone
365	- Updates `~/.flow/config.toml` with `mode = "develop"`, `source_target = <clone-path>`, and installed_at

369	### `flow update`
370	
371	Roll forward a release install to the latest semver tag from the configured remote.
372	
373	In release mode:
374	
375	- Calls `git ls-remote --tags --refs` against the configured remote
376	- Picks the highest semver-ish tag (`vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH[-suffix]`)
377	- Clones that tag into a temp directory
378	- Stages and validates the new content, then atomically swaps into `~/.flow/source/`
379	- Updates `~/.flow/config.toml` with the new version and installed_at
380	
381	In develop mode: prints the manual `git pull` + `flow sync ... --user` commands; takes no other action.
382	
383	Flags:
384	
385	- `--check` — report current vs latest version without applying. When a newer version is available, also fetches `CHANGELOG.md` from the remote at the new tag (via a sparse partial-clone — only the one file is actually downloaded) and prints the `## [<version>]` section so you can see what's in the available release. Falls back silently if no CHANGELOG entry exists for that version.
386	- `--resync` — after applying, also run `flow sync claude --user` and `flow sync codex --user`
387	- `--remote URL` — override the remote configured in `~/.flow/config.toml` (useful for testing)
388	- `--json` — with `--check`, emit classified update diagnostics for support automation
389	
390	The update is atomic: staging is validated before any rename happens, so a failed clone, broken staging, or swap error leaves the existing install intact. A successful update keeps no rollback state — to revert, run `flow update --remote <url>` against an older tag or re-run `install-flow.sh --release` from a checkout at the desired version.

428	### `flow harvest claude`
429	
430	Read Claude Code session transcripts from `~/.claude/projects/` into the usage store's raw layer at `~/.flow/usage.db`.
431	
432	Behavior:
433	
434	- incremental — resumes from the last-read position per file, so re-running is cheap
435	- writes session and turn records; reads nothing over the network
436	- creates the store on first use
437	
438	Flags:
439	
440	- `--rescan` — rewind already-recorded files' watermarks first and re-read them from the start
441	- `--since DATE` — with `--rescan`, only rewind files modified on or after `DATE` (`YYYY-MM-DD` or a full ISO timestamp)
442	- `--session ID` — with `--rescan`, only rewind files whose path contains `ID`
443	- `--dry-run` — with `--rescan`, report the scope and exit without writing anything
444	
445	Use this when you want the store current before a read-only cost view. `flow cost active` and `flow cost verdict` run the relevant live harvest path for their own surfaces.
446	
447	#### When you need `--rescan`
448	
449	A plain harvest only reads what is new since last time, so a collector improvement never reaches transcripts already on disk. `--rescan` re-reads them. Three things only it can recover:
450	
451	- **full output-token counts.** A streamed response is written as several transcript lines that share one request id, and only the last carries the final `output_tokens`. Collectors before v3 kept the first, storing a partial count — about a third of the real output, measured against the console.
452	- **compaction events.** `compact_boundary` records were dropped entirely before collector v3.
453	- **titles, `cwd`, and title provenance** for sessions harvested before those were captured.
454	
455	Safe to run repeatedly. The output-token rule is highest-wins, which is order-independent, so a rescan cannot un-correct a row it already fixed.
456	
457	Rescanning the whole corpus re-reads every recorded transcript. Rehearse the filters first:
458	
459	```
460	flow harvest claude --rescan --since 2026-08-01 --dry-run
461	flow harvest claude --rescan --since 2026-08-01
462	```
463	
464	`--session` takes a session uuid and matches it against file paths, which reaches that session's main transcript and its subagent files together.
465	
466	A transcript deleted from disk cannot be rescanned — its stored turns keep whatever the collector recorded at the time, permanently.
467	
468	`--backfill` is the former name of `--rescan` and still works. It is hidden from `--help`; prefer `--rescan`.
469

471	
472	Read Codex session transcripts from `~/.codex/sessions/` into the usage store's raw layer. No flags.
473	
474	Behavior:
475	
476	- incremental and resumable, the same as the Claude harvest
477	- `flow cost active` runs this automatically when `~/.codex/sessions/` exists, because active status is a current-state view
478	- read-only views do not run it; they report freshness and name the manual refresh path when Codex data may be stale

483	
484	Project every harness's raw turn records into one shared token convention.
485	
486	Behavior:
487	
488	- only rows without a current-version normalized counterpart are recomputed, so this is safe and cheap to re-run
489	
490	Use this after a manual harvest, before reading `cost summary`, `cost sessions`, `cost trend`, or `cost baseline`. `flow cost active` and `flow cost verdict` normalize for their own current-state reads.

492	### `flow cost summary`
493	
494	Token totals grouped by harness and model, plus the most recent Codex capacity reading as a separate gauge line.
495	
496	Flags:
497	
498	- `--days N` — show the last N days (default: 7)
499	- `--all` — show every row ever normalized; cannot be combined with `--days`
500	- `--json` — print the same result as JSON instead of an aligned table
501	
502	Reads only the normalized layer — it does not harvest, so what it shows is as current as your last harvest/normalize pass. It includes freshness metadata in JSON and a freshness note in text output when the store is empty, stale, partial, or unreadable. Prints `(no data in range)` when the window is empty.
503	
504	**The capacity line is a snapshot with an expiry.** It renders the reading's own `resets at` time beside `as of`, and it disappears entirely once that time passes — an expired gauge is absent, not dimmed. Primary and secondary expire independently. A reading sampled more than halfway through its own window is still shown, with a note: it is valid, but usage has had most of the window to move since.
505	
506	### `flow cost trend`
507	
508	Efficiency per time bucket — the view that answers "is my session hygiene actually working," which the level-reporting views cannot.
509	
510	One row per **bucket and harness**, not per bucket. Blending them would mean summing token classes whose semantics differ: Codex's cached input is a subset of its input, where Claude's cache buckets are disjoint and additive.
511	
512	Flags:
513	
514	- `--days N` — show the last N days (default: 7)
515	- `--all` — every row ever normalized; cannot be combined with `--days`
516	- `--bucket day|week` — bucket size (default: day)
517	- `--harness claude|codex` — restrict to one harness (default: both)
518	- `--json` — JSON instead of an aligned table
519	
520	Columns:
521	
522	| Column | Meaning |
523	|---|---|
524	| `turns` | main-agent turns (sidechains excluded) |
525	| `sessions` | distinct sessions with a main-agent turn in the bucket |
526	| `ctx/turn` | mean context per main-agent turn |
527	| `in:out` | total input over total output |
528	| `wt/1k out` | **weighted tokens per 1,000 output** — the headline |
529	| `sub%` | subagent share of weighted tokens |
530	| `cmpct man` / `cmpct auto` | compaction events, split by trigger |
531	| `med pre man` | median context at the point of a manual `/compact` |
532	
533	`wt/1k out` collapses the input classes by billing multiplier (uncached 1.0, cache read 0.1, 5m write 1.25, 1h write 2.0) and divides by output. Dividing by output is what makes it an efficiency number rather than a busyness number — raw daily burn conflates working less with working leaner. The multipliers live in `data/token_weights.json`, so a pricing change is a data edit rather than a release.
534	
535	`wt/1k out` and `sub%` are blank for Codex. The weights are Anthropic cache multipliers, Codex reports no cache writes at all, and its cache-read semantics differ — the same arithmetic would not mean the same thing.
536	
537	Manual and auto compactions are never summed. A manual `/compact` is deliberate hygiene; an auto one is hitting the ceiling. They are opposite signals about a session's health, and `med pre man` is the useful companion: how full the context typically was when you chose to cut.
538	
539	**Buckets follow your local calendar, not UTC.** Stored timestamps are UTC and every window comparison stays UTC, but a bucket is a label on a human day: bucketing by UTC splits an evening across two rows for anyone west of Greenwich, and on the corpus this was built against that moved 7% of a week's turns off the day they happened. A week is keyed by its **Monday's date** rather than a week number — `%W` counts weeks within a calendar year, so a week spanning New Year would otherwise split into two partial buckets and skew every volume column.
540	
541	Read-only, and it does not harvest first — a trend over completed periods does not become wrong for want of the last few minutes.
542	
543	**Coverage is labelled, never silently truncated.** If the window reaches back before the earliest harvested turn for a harness, a note says so. Absent buckets and empty buckets are different facts, and hiding the difference turns a coverage gap into a false trend.
544	
545	### `flow cost baseline`
546	
547	The always-on token floor — what a session costs to *open*, before any work happens — and the changes that moved it.
548	
549	Every session pays a static prefix: system prompt, tool definitions, MCP server instructions, agent and skill descriptions, `CLAUDE.md`, memory files. Every other `cost` view measures what a session spent; this one measures where it started. The distinction matters because enabling a plugin raises the opening cost of every future session, permanently and invisibly.
550	
551	Flags:
552	
553	- `--days N` — show the last N days (default: 7)
554	- `--all` — every bucket ever normalized; **this is the useful invocation**, since a changepoint log needs more than one bucket to compare
555	- `--harness claude|codex` — restrict to one harness (default: both)
556	- `--by-cwd` — estimate per working directory instead of pooling, one block per directory
557	- `--json` — JSON instead of the rendered block
558	
559	**The estimator is `cache_read_tokens` on a session's first turn.** At that point no conversation exists, so the number is the cached static prefix and nothing else — the opening message and any SessionStart hook output land in `fresh_input_tokens` instead. The obvious alternative, `fresh + cache_read + cache_write`, is available on more sessions but reads high for exactly that reason.
560	
561	A session qualifies only when all four hold. Each rule removes a different way a turn can look like a first turn without being one:
562	
563	| Rule | Removes |
564	|---|---|
565	| minimum `turn_seq` among non-subagent turns | a subagent turn that precedes the main thread in the file |
566	| `source_line_no` at or below the threshold | sessions where the collector first attached mid-file, so its earliest row is mid-conversation |
567	| no `compact_boundary` at or before the turn | resumed sessions, which restart with a summary already in context |
568	| `cache_read_tokens > 0` | cache misses, which carry no prefix reading at all |
569	
570	`cache_read_tokens = 0` means **cache miss, not new conversation.** The prompt cache is keyed by prefix hash across the account rather than per session, so a genuinely new session started soon after another with the same prefix reads the whole thing from cache. Those are the good observations here.
571	
572	**Reported at p10, not a mid-range quantile.** Prefix readings are not a distribution — they are a few exact, repeated plateaus, because the cache returns the same number for every session sharing a prefix. One measured week had all 13 of its sessions read 22,489; another had all 41 read 21,830. When two configurations coexist in a week, a mid-range quantile tracks the *mix* between plateaus rather than the floor, and jumps when the mix shifts. On the corpus this was built against, p25 manufactured a +35% spike and a −28% return across weeks in which nothing changed. p10 is flat there, and equals the minimum in every measured week.
573	
574	**A change registers only when it clears both 15% and 2,500 tokens.** Either bound alone misfires at one end of the range. The consequence is stated in the output rather than hidden: a change smaller than that is invisible here. This detects deliberate reconfiguration, not gradual creep — one plugin quietly returning will not show up.
575	
576	**Changes are detected within a series, never across two.** Pooled, that is one series over time. Under `--by-cwd` it is one series per directory, each with its own headline and history — two directories in the same week are not a sequence, and comparing them would report the gap between two projects as a change over time.
577	
578	**Both endpoints of a change are shown, and skipped weeks are marked.** Buckets exist only for weeks that had observations, so two adjacent rows can be months apart. A change reported as `2026-06-22 -> 2026-07-06` with a "weeks skipped" note happened somewhere in that span, not necessarily in the later week.
579	
580	Pooled across projects by default. `--by-cwd` is available but fragments the population quickly: on the corpus this was built against, 166 observations spread over 24 directories left only three with 20 or more. It is also largely unnecessary — the floor's dominant contributors are global, and the three directories with enough observations to compare agreed to within 6%.
581	
582	The pooled figure has a known sensitivity, disclosed in its own output: it reports the *leanest project's* prefix, so a week that adds sessions from a lighter directory lowers it without any configuration changing. This is the same failure mode that ruled out p25, one level up, and it can only be disclosed rather than filtered away.
583	
584	`compaction filtering:` distinguishes capability from coverage. A store harvested before the collector began recording `compact_boundary` has the capability and no rows, and says so rather than claiming a filter that matched nothing.
585	
586	A bucket below the minimum sample keeps its row and its count but reports no floor. A thin week and a week with no sessions are different facts, and a quantile over a handful of sessions is noise dressed as a measurement.
587	
588	No `~` markers. Unlike an inferred context window, every figure here is a value some session actually reported.
589	
590	Read-only, no harvest, no schema. Like every other `cost` surface, it measures this machine only.
591	
592	### `flow cost sessions`
593	
594	Token totals grouped by session, most recently active first.
595	
596	Flags:
597	
598	- `--days N` — show the last N days (default: 7)
599	- `--all` — every row ever normalized; cannot be combined with `--days`
600	- `--json` — JSON instead of an aligned table
601	- `--limit N` — cap the sessions shown (default: 20; `0` = unlimited)
